title: One database query causes 90% of production database CPU
description: Diagnose and fix a single database query that consumes 90% of production database CPU by analyzing execution plans, adding indexes, and query rewriting.

data.text: Your production database CPU spikes to 95% during peak hours. The slow query log reveals one query accounting for 90% of total CPU time. The query joins three large tables and returns a paginated result set. You need to optimize it without changing the application behavior or breaking existing functionality.

items: Enable the slow query log with a low threshold (e.g., 100ms) to capture the offending query
Use pg_stat_statements (PostgreSQL) or sys.dm_exec_query_stats (SQL Server) to find the top CPU consumer
Obtain the execution plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE or SQL Server Management Studio
Look for full table scans, missing index warnings, or nested loops with high row estimates
Correlate the query text with application code to understand the intent and access pattern

terms.definition: The step-by-step plan the database optimizer chooses to execute a query, including index usage and join strategies.
A pattern where N+1 separate queries are executed instead of one joined query, causing excessive database round trips.
Reading every row in a table to find matching rows, which is slow on large tables without indexes.
An index that contains all columns required by a query, allowing the database to satisfy the query from the index alone.
A cache of execution plans reused for identical queries to avoid recompilation overhead.

items: Add a covering index for the query's WHERE, JOIN, and SELECT columns
Rewrite the query to eliminate unnecessary joins or columns
Add pagination with keyset criteria instead of OFFSET for deep pages
Materialize expensive aggregations in a summary table refreshed on a schedule
Introduce caching at the application layer for frequently accessed results
Fix N+1 queries by using eager loading or a single joined query

cards.title: Indexing
cards.description: Add B-tree or covering indexes to speed up lookups and joins.

cards.title: Query rewriting
cards.description: Restructure the SQL to use more efficient joins, filters, or subqueries.
cons: Harder to maintain if logic is complex

cards.title: Caching layer
cards.description: Store query results in Redis or application memory to reduce database load.

cards.title: Materialized view
cards.description: Pre-compute and store the query result for fast reads.

data.title: Execution plan showing a table scan
data.content: PostgreSQL EXPLAIN ANALYZE reveals a sequential scan on a 10M row table:
data.code:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT o.id, o.total, c.name
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
ORDER BY o.created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- Output:
-- Limit (cost=0.00..1856.44 rows=20 width=48)
--   ->  Merge Join (cost=0.00..1856.44 rows=20 width=48)
--         Merge Cond: (o.customer_id = c.id)
--         ->  Index Scan using idx_orders_created on orders o
--         ->  Seq Scan on customers c  -- Full table scan!
--               Filter: (id IS NOT NULL)

data.caption: Query optimization workflow from detection to fix
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[High CPU alert] --> B[Check slow query log]
    B --> C[Identify top CPU query]
    C --> D[Get execution plan]
    D --> E{Missing index?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Add covering index]
    E -->|No| G{Full table scan?}
    G -->|Yes| H[Add index or rewrite query]
    G -->|No| I{Inefficient join?}
    I -->|Yes| J[Rewrite join or add index]
    I -->|No| K[Check for N+1 in app code]
    F --> L[Verify CPU drops]
    H --> L
    J --> L
    K --> L

data.title: Index selectivity matters
data.text: An index on a column with low selectivity (e.g., boolean or enum with two values) will not help. The database optimizer may still choose a table scan. Index columns with high cardinality and use them in WHERE and JOIN clauses.

data.title: Optimize a slow query
data.description: Given a slow query and its execution plan, identify the bottleneck and implement a fix.
steps: Obtain the execution plan for the provided slow query
Identify the operator with the highest cost or execution time
Determine whether an index, query rewrite, or caching strategy is most appropriate
Implement the fix in a development database
Re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to verify the improvement
data.expectedOutcome: You should reduce the query cost by at least 80% and eliminate full table scans.

data.title: Summary
points: Use the slow query log or query stats to identify the top CPU consumer
Analyze the execution plan for table scans and missing indexes
Add covering indexes for high-frequency queries
Fix N+1 problems in application code before tuning individual queries
data.takeaway: A single unoptimized query can dominate database CPU. Always profile before and after any change to verify the impact.
